en: Udāna 6.4 Paṭhamanānātitthiyasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, many ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects were residing in Sāvatthī, holding various views, various convictions, various inclinations, and relying on various doctrinal positions.
Among them, some ascetics and brahmins held such doctrines and such views:
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
“The world is non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false.
But there are also some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The world is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
There are some recluses and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The soul is the same as the body; this alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
"The soul is one thing, the body is another; this alone is true, all else is false.
There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The Tathāgata exists after death; this alone is true, all else is false.
Yet there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false.”
There are some recluses and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view:
“The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.
Yet there are other recluses and brahmins who hold this doctrine and this view:
“The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.
Having become contentious, quarrelsome, and engaged in disputes, they dwell piercing one another with the weapons of their tongues, saying:
“The Dhamma is thus, the Dhamma is not thus!”
“Such is the Dhamma, such is the Dhamma.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after their meal, returning from their almsround, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:

"Here, Bhante, many ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of various sects are residing in Sāvatthī, holding various views, various inclinations, various preferences, and relying on various doctrinal positions.
Among them, some ascetics and brahmins speak thus and hold such a view: [text continues]"

‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’ … [and so on] … Having become engaged in quarrels, strife, and disputes, they dwell piercing one another with the weapons of the mouth, saying:
‘The Dhamma is like this, it is not like that.’
“Such is the Dhamma, such is the Dhamma.
“Bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless;
they do not know what is beneficial, they do not know what is harmful, they do not know what is the Dhamma, and they do not know what is non-Dhamma.”

Not knowing what is beneficial, not knowing what is harmful, not knowing what is Dhamma, and not knowing what is non-Dhamma, they live engaged in quarrels, disputes, and arguments, piercing one another with the weapons of the tongue, saying:
"The Dhamma is like this, it is not like that;
the Dhamma is not like this, it is like that."
“Once upon a time, monks, there was a certain king in this very Sāvatthī.
Then, monks, that king addressed a certain man, saying:
‘Come, good man, assemble together all those who are born blind in Sāvatthī.’”
‘Yes, sire,’ that man replied to the king, monks, and having gathered all the people born blind in Sāvatthī, he approached the king. Having approached, he said this to the king:
‘Sire, all those born blind in Sāvatthī have been assembled.
‘In that case, my good man, show an elephant to the blind men.’
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ the man replied to the king, and he showed the elephant to the people blind from birth.
To some of those blind from birth he showed the elephant’s head, saying:
‘Such, O blind ones, is the elephant.’
To some of the blind men he showed the elephant’s ear, saying:
“Such, blind men, is the elephant.
To some of the blind men he showed the elephant’s tusk, saying:
“Such, blind men, is an elephant,” he said.
To some of the blind men he showed the trunk of the elephant:
“Such, blind men, is an elephant.”
To some of the blind men he showed the body of the elephant, saying:
"Such, O blind men, is the elephant.
To some of the blind men he showed the foot of the elephant:
“Such, blind men, is an elephant,” he said.
To some of the blind men he showed the elephant’s thigh, saying:
“Such, blind men, is an elephant.”
To some of the blind men he showed the elephant’s tail, saying:
“Such, O blind men, is the elephant.
To some of the blind men he showed the elephant’s tail-hair.
‘Such, O congenitally blind ones, is an elephant.
Then, monks, that man, having shown the elephant to the congenitally blind, approached the king; having approached, he said this to the king:
‘Your majesty, those congenitally blind have seen the elephant.’”
"Now, do as you think fit," he said.
Then, monks, that king approached those people blind from birth; having approached them, he said to those born blind:
"Have you seen the elephant, blind men?"
‘Thus, Your Majesty, we have seen the elephant.
‘Tell me, you who were born blind, what kind of thing is an elephant?
Those among the blind men, bhikkhus, by whom the head of the elephant had been seen, spoke thus: [“It is like a jar.”]
“‘Such, Your Majesty, is the elephant, just like a water-jar,’ they said.
Those among the blind men from birth who had seen the elephant’s ear, bhikkhus, said:
‘Such, Your Majesty, is the elephant, just like a winnowing-basket.’”
“Bhikkhus, those among the blind from birth who had seen the elephant’s tusk said:
‘Your Majesty, the elephant is just like a wooden post.
Those among the blind from birth who had seen the elephant’s trunk said:”
“‘Such, O King, is the elephant; it is just like a plough-pole,’ they said.
But those congenitally blind men among them who had touched the elephant’s body, monks, spoke thus:
‘Such, O King, is the elephant; it is just like a granary.’”
“Bhikkhus, those among the blind from birth who had seen the elephant’s foot said:
‘Sire, the elephant is like a pillar.
Those among the blind from birth who had seen the elephant’s thigh said:”
“‘Such, O King, is the elephant, just like a mortar,’ said those,
monks, among the blind-born who had seen the elephant’s tail:
‘Such, O King, is the elephant, just like a pestle.’”
“Bhikkhus, those among the blind men who had touched the elephant’s tail said:
‘Sire, the elephant is like a broom. They said:
‘The elephant is like this, not like that;’”
‘The elephant is not like this; the elephant is like that,’ they struck one another with their fists.
And because of that, monks, the king was pleased.
In the same way, monks, the wanderers of other sects are blind and sightless.
They do not know what is beneficial, they do not know what is harmful; they do not know what is Dhamma, they do not know what is non-Dhamma.

Not knowing what is beneficial, not knowing what is harmful, not knowing what is Dhamma, and not knowing what is non-Dhamma, they live engaged in quarrels, disputes, and contention, piercing one another with the weapons of the tongue:
“The Dhamma is like this; the Dhamma is not like that.”
‘Such is the Dhamma, such is the Dhamma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the significance of this, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“It seems they are attached to these things...”
"Some ascetics and brahmins,
grasping at their own views, dispute with one another,
seeing only a single side."
The fourth.
